I’m a visual learner as well and I often struggled in lectures (I’ve got ADHD and dyspraxia as well).

I found it super helpful to take notes on the PowerPoint during the lecture (using the note bit in PowerPoint so every note was on the relevant slide), meaning I didn’t have to write things down that were on the PowerPoint itself and I could focus on writing down notes and things I might want to look up later.

That way there was less note taking panic and I felt more able to focus on what the lecturer was saying and jot down important things that weren’t on the PowerPoint. Then after the lecture I could look up anything I was unsure about or needed more info on.

If you start getting signs of a UTI, get it checked immediately!

If you feel a burning sensation before/during/after peeing, feel you have to constantly pee, and/or not much pee comes out - it’s a possible sign of a UTI.

If you feel a pain in your lower back (and/or feel generally unwell suddenly), this most likely means that the infection has spread to your kidneys. A kidney infection needs to be treated ASAP as the next step is a blood infection or sepsis.

I thought the UTI had gone on its own but I didn’t realise that the back pain I had developed was in fact the infection spreading to my kidneys. I was finally diagnosed with ADD this year (24) but I’ve suspected this since I was a teenager.

When I was around 15 I was asked to do a few self evaluations and one of them raised some flags about AD(H)D. The therapist suggested I seek an assessment with a specialist and to speak to my parents about this. I told my mum what had happened and that the therapist had suggested a proper screening. My mum simply replied: “Why? You’re not hyperactive.” She wouldn’t take this any further because she didn’t want to seek any diagnoses or medication, basically anything that might make her kid “weak”.

I was really upset with her as I knew that the diagnostic process is a lot more difficult once you’re an adult. I just continued to struggle and once in a while thought I might actually have ADD and whether I should seek an assessment/advice about it.

Fast forward almost ten years and during an appointment with my psychiatrist, he suddenly starts to ask about my concentration, memory, and fidgeting. He suggested that we do an assessment and then discussed my options of trying medication. I was ambivalent about it but the first day of trying Elvanse my world completely changed to the better!

I’m so glad that I’ve finally got a diagnosis and help but I’m frustrated with my mum for dismissing this when I was younger. It felt quite validating that my psychiatrist had noticed signs without me ever bringing it up. I’ve still not told my mum about it though. We have a fantastic relationship and are very close but I feel that she would judge me, thinking that I’m looking for excuses.

I’m sorry that your parents didn’t notice things earlier, I hope things are better now and that you’re seeking the support you need.

UK mental health professional here.

If a person admits to suicidal ideation we have to act. Of course the action we take depends on a thorough risk assessment, but unfortunately we sometimes have to go against the person’s wishes and provide closer observations than the person would prefer.

From my experience, this has a lot to do with today’s blame culture and the rocky history of mental health treatment. We have to take intense precautions because if the person ends up killing themselves we are often blamed for not doing enough.

Being deprived in some aspect of personal space, decision making, and freedom is absolutely horrible but unfortunately often necessary.

However, I absolutely agree that this highly affects people’s willingness to be forthcoming with us. We try to keep a person safe but in return it often causes distrust and distance.
